# The subtleties of the principles in the Northern section

<margin>Feeding at the breast</margin>
The child feeding at the breast of its dead mother, after a short while, looks as if it has lost her, and <margin>This means that at the blink of an eye, the mother is gone</margin>
rising, it does not see her. It does not find anyone who resembles her. That which you loved in your mother was <margin>The stiffening of the body no longer resembles her</margin>
<margin>If the form is not worth loving, then there is nothing left to love</margin>
not her physical form, but that which moved her form. When men die in battle, they are buried; <margin>When they die in battle, there is no value in physical strength, therefore one does not provide them with concubines</margin>
yet one does not provide them with concubines to be killed as funerary offerings. The fetus, in its repeated states, has no conscious intention; to love it is to lose <margin>Repeatedly returning to the foundation/root</margin>
<margin>Another metaphor: To select concubines without exhausting their complete form, so as to avoid inflicting harm on the supreme nobility</margin>
its foundation. Those who are the concubines of the Son of Heaven do not have their nails trimmed, nor their ears pierced. Those who take <margin>They are not placed in official labor, for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would make them unfit for the intimate duties of the newlywed</margin>
wives are stopped at the outer gates. Even when one is not permitted to employ them again, if the form is complete, it is still sufficient to move <margin>Those whose form is complete are still sufficient to move others</margin>
the mind.
The mind below is again this.

<meta>De Chong Fu (The Sign of Virtue Complete)</meta>
<meta>Richuan Tang (Sun and River Hall)</meta>

<summary>This passage discusses the distinction between physical form and the underlying essence of life, using the metaphors of a nursing infant and the treatment of imperial concubines to argue that true worth resides in the wholeness of the individual rather than external utility.</summary>
<keywords>Zhuangzi, De Chong Fu, physical form, essence of life, internal nature, wholeness</keywords>
